title: Why is `finalize()` deprecated (unpredictable timing, resurrection, double-GC, swallowed exceptions), and how does `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` (Java 9+) replace it safely?
shortTitle: Why is finalize() deprecated, and how does java.lang.ref.Cleaner replace it safely?

s1_definition.profdef: The `Object.finalize()` method was a callback the garbage collector invoked before reclaiming an object, intended to let the object release native resources. It is deprecated because its timing is unpredictable, it can resurrect objects and force a second collection cycle, it silently swallows exceptions, it harms performance, and it provides no guarantee of ever running. The modern replacement is `java.lang.ref.Cleaner`, introduced in Java 9, which registers a separate cleanup action tied to an object's reachability through a phantom reference, runs that action on a dedicated cleaner thread after the object becomes unreachable, and critically does not give the cleanup action any reference to the object itself, so resurrection is impossible.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India had an old rule that when a safe-deposit locker is abandoned, the locker itself is supposed to lock its own door on the way out. That is finalize: the dying object cleans up after itself. The problem is the locker might lock late, might never lock, and worse, in the act of "locking" it could grab back its own contents and come alive again, confusing the whole vault. The Cleaner approach is to hire a dedicated janitor who holds only a cleanup ticket, never the locker's contents, and who is told "when locker 12 is truly abandoned, run this shutdown checklist." The janitor cannot accidentally revive the locker because he never had its contents, only the ticket.
s1_definition.oneliner: finalize runs unpredictably, can resurrect objects, swallows exceptions, and may never run; Cleaner runs a resource-only cleanup action on a dedicated thread after the object is gone, with no way to revive it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The `Object.finalize()` method was a callback the garbage collector invoked before reclaiming an object, intended to let the object release native resources. It is deprecated because its timing is unpredictable, it can resurrect objects and force a second collection cycle, it silently swallows exceptions, it harms performance, and it provides no guarantee of ever running. The modern replacement is `java.lang.ref.Cleaner`, introduced in Java 9, which registers a separate cleanup action tied to an object's reachability through a phantom reference, runs that action on a dedicated cleaner thread after the object becomes unreachable, and critically does not give the cleanup action any reference to the object itself, so resurrection is impossible.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India had an old rule that when a safe-deposit locker is abandoned, the locker itself is supposed to lock its own door on the way out. That is finalize: the dying object cleans up after itself. The problem is the locker might lock late, might never lock, and worse, in the act of "locking" it could grab back its own contents and come alive again, confusing the whole vault. The Cleaner approach is to hire a dedicated janitor who holds only a cleanup ticket, never the locker's contents, and who is told "when locker 12 is truly abandoned, run this shutdown checklist." The janitor cannot accidentally revive the locker because he never had its contents, only the ticket.

**One line to remember:** finalize runs unpredictably, can resurrect objects, swallows exceptions, and may never run; Cleaner runs a resource-only cleanup action on a dedicated thread after the object is gone, with no way to revive it.

sections.s2_technical:
The original idea behind finalize was reasonable: an object holding a native resource, such as a file handle or an off-heap buffer, could override finalize so that if the programmer forgot to close it, the garbage collector would eventually call finalize and the resource would be released. In practice this mechanism is deeply flawed, which is why it has been deprecated since Java 9 and is being removed.

The first flaw is unpredictable timing. finalize runs only when the garbage collector decides the object is unreachable and gets around to processing its finalization queue. There is no bound on how long that takes, so a native resource like a database connection might stay open for minutes or hours after the object is logically dead, which in a connection-limited banking system can exhaust the pool and halt transactions.

The second flaw is that there is no guarantee finalize ever runs at all. If the program exits, or the collector never needs to reclaim that object, finalize may simply never be called, so you cannot rely on it to release anything critical.

The third flaw is resurrection. Because finalize receives the object as `this`, the finalizer can store `this` into a static field or some live collection, making the object reachable again. The garbage collector then cannot reclaim it, and because an object's finalize is only ever run once, after resurrection it will never be finalized again even when it dies a second time. This also forces a double collection cycle: an object with a finalizer cannot be reclaimed in the collection that first finds it unreachable; it must survive one cycle to be finalized and only be reclaimed in a later cycle, which pressures the collector and promotes garbage into older generations.

The fourth flaw is that any exception thrown inside finalize is swallowed. The garbage collector catches and discards it, so a bug in cleanup produces no stack trace and no error, making failures invisible. Combined with the performance cost, since finalizable objects take a slower allocation and collection path, finalize is considered actively harmful.

The replacement is java.lang.ref.Cleaner. You create a single shared Cleaner, typically one per class or per application, with `Cleaner.create()`. For each resource-holding object you register a cleanup action with `cleaner.register(obj, runnable)`, which returns a `Cleaner.Cleanable` you can also invoke explicitly. The crucial design rule is that the registered Runnable must not hold any reference to the object being cleaned, because the Cleaner tracks the object with a phantom reference, and if the cleanup action captured the object it would keep it alive and never fire. So you put the native resource state into a separate static nested class that implements Runnable, holding only the handle to release, never the outer object. When the outer object becomes phantom-reachable, the Cleaner enqueues it and runs the action on its own dedicated daemon thread. Because the action never had the object, resurrection is impossible, and exceptions in the action can be handled properly on the cleaner thread.

The senior-level guidance is that Cleaner is still only a safety net, not a primary mechanism. The correct primary pattern remains implementing AutoCloseable and using try-with-resources so the resource is released deterministically at a known point. The Cleaner is the backstop for the case where a caller forgets to close, exactly as finalize was intended to be, but without finalize's defects. In the finance domain you would combine both: a class holding a native handle implements AutoCloseable for deterministic release and registers a Cleaner as insurance.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a market-data component that opens a native off-heap buffer for each price feed subscription. Originally it relied on finalize to free the buffer. Under load the feeds were logically closed but their native buffers lingered for a long time because finalize ran whenever the collector felt like it, and native memory grew until the process was killed. This is exactly the unpredictable-timing flaw of finalize: the resource is not released at a known point, so it accumulates.

Problem 2 — The team needs deterministic release when the subscription is closed normally, plus a guaranteed safety net that frees the buffer if a caller forgets to close, and that safety net must never accidentally revive the subscription object. This is exactly what the AutoCloseable plus Cleaner combination provides: try-with-resources frees the buffer immediately in the normal path, and the Cleaner frees it later as insurance without any reference back to the object.

We will build a runnable demo modelling a PriceFeedSubscription that holds a simulated native buffer. It implements AutoCloseable for deterministic close and registers a Cleaner with a resource-only state holder. The demo shows the deterministic close path with try-with-resources and the safety-net path where close is forgotten and the Cleaner eventually fires. The code includes the subscription class, a static nested BufferState Runnable that holds only the native handle, a shared Cleaner, and a demo main exercising both paths.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two price feed subscriptions, one used inside try-with-resources and one deliberately leaked.

Step 1: At start the open native buffer count is zero.

Step 2: The first subscription for RELIANCE is created inside a try-with-resources block, which increments the open buffer count to one and registers a Cleaner action holding only the buffer and symbol, never the subscription object.

Step 3: When the try block ends, close is called automatically, which invokes the Cleanable, runs BufferState, frees the native buffer, and decrements the count back to zero. This is the deterministic path, and it happens at a known point.

Step 4: The leaked subscription for TCS is created inside a helper method and never closed. The open buffer count rises to one again, but when the method returns the subscription becomes unreachable.

Step 5: The demo nudges the garbage collector. Once the subscription is phantom-reachable, the Cleaner enqueues it, and the dedicated cleaner thread runs BufferState, which frees the buffer and decrements the count to zero. Because BufferState never held the subscription, the object could die normally and could not be resurrected.

Step 6: The final count is zero, proving both the deterministic path and the safety-net path released the resource, with no finalize method anywhere and no exceptions swallowed.

```
2026-10-30 17:50:11 INFO    Open native buffers at start: 0
2026-10-30 17:50:11 INFO    Using RELIANCE feed, handle=1001, open buffers=1
2026-10-30 17:50:11 INFO    Freed native buffer for feed RELIANCE (handle=1001)
2026-10-30 17:50:11 INFO    After try-with-resources, open buffers: 0
2026-10-30 17:50:11 WARNING Created TCS feed but FORGOT to close it, handle=2002
2026-10-30 17:50:12 INFO    Freed native buffer for feed TCS (handle=2002)
2026-10-30 17:50:12 WARNING After GC safety net, open buffers: 0 (Cleaner released the forgotten buffer — no finalize, no resurrection)
```

```text
  new PriceFeedSubscription("RELIANCE")
    │ NativeBuffer reserved (openCount=1)
    │ CLEANER.register(this, BufferState(buffer,symbol))  ← no 'this' captured
    ▼
  ┌─ DETERMINISTIC PATH ──────────┐  ┌─ SAFETY-NET PATH ─────────────┐
  │ try-with-resources ends       │  │ caller forgets close()        │
  │  → close() → cleanable.clean()│  │  → object becomes unreachable │
  │  → BufferState.run()          │  │  → phantom-reachable          │
  │  → buffer.free() NOW          │  │  → Cleaner thread runs        │
  │  openCount 1 → 0              │  │  → BufferState.run()          │
  │                               │  │  → buffer.free() LATER        │
  └───────────────────────────────┘  │  openCount 1 → 0              │
                                      └───────────────────────────────┘
  No finalize → no resurrection, no swallowed exceptions, no double-GC
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The finalize method was a garbage-collector callback meant to let an object release native resources if the programmer forgot, but it is deprecated since Java 9 because it is unreliable and dangerous in several specific ways. Its timing is unpredictable, so a native resource like a buffer or connection can linger long after the object is logically dead, which in a connection-limited banking system can exhaust the pool. It offers no guarantee of ever running, because if the object is never reclaimed or the program exits, finalize simply never fires. It allows resurrection, because the finalizer receives the object as this and can store it somewhere live, reviving it, and since finalize runs at most once, the object can then never be finalized again. It forces a double collection cycle, since finalizable objects survive the first collection and are only reclaimed later, which promotes garbage and pressures the collector. And it swallows exceptions, so a cleanup bug produces no stack trace and fails invisibly.

The modern replacement is java.lang.ref.Cleaner, added in Java 9. You create one shared Cleaner, and for each resource-holding object you register a cleanup action. The Cleaner tracks the object with a phantom reference and runs the action on a dedicated daemon thread once the object becomes unreachable. The single most important rule is that the cleanup action must not hold any reference to the object it cleans, because such a reference would keep the object alive and the action would never fire. So you put the resource state into a separate class that holds only the native handle, never the owning object, which also makes resurrection structurally impossible since the action never had the object to revive.

In a project at National Bank of India we had a market-data component that opened an off-heap native buffer per price-feed subscription and originally relied on finalize to free it. Under load the native memory grew uncontrollably because finalize ran whenever the collector felt like it, and the process was eventually killed. We rewrote the subscription to implement AutoCloseable so the normal path frees the buffer deterministically through try-with-resources at a known point, and we registered a Cleaner as a safety net holding only the buffer, so that if a caller forgot to close, the buffer would still be freed later without any risk of reviving the subscription.

The principle I always state is that the primary mechanism for native resources is deterministic release through AutoCloseable and try-with-resources, and the Cleaner is only a backstop for forgotten closes, exactly the role finalize was meant to play but without any of its defects. I never write a finalize method, I make cleanup actions idempotent so they are safe whether triggered by an explicit close or by the cleaner thread, and I keep the cleanup state completely free of back-references to the owning object. That gives deterministic cleanup in the common case, a guaranteed safety net in the forgotten case, no resurrection, no swallowed exceptions, and no double collection penalty.
